messages.author: a73b025ad2f2853f
messages.subject: batch effect MSstats handled ?
parts:
Hi,
  Trying to figure out if MSstats is handling batch effect?  Not sure. According to doc
https://mirrors.dotsrc.org/bioconductor-releases/3.12/bioc/manuals/MSstats/man/MSstats.pdf

 p3
dataProcess()  method perform:
 Normalization: to remove systematic bias between MS runs.

Is that not definition of batch effect? I want to know if I apply dataProcess() Normalization, I actually do batch effect correction ?

Many thanks!

messages.author: 13904eb0f06097b0
messages.subject: Re: batch effect MSstats handled ?
parts:
Hello,

Yep normalization will handle catch effects. The default option is to equalize medians across runs.

Devon

messages.author: 3f7dab23a7bc0436
messages.subject: Re: batch effect MSstats handled ?
parts:
Hi Ju,

One additional note to point out - your normalization strategy depends on your assumptions.  For example, median normalization assumes most of the proteins in the experiment are the same and have the same concentration for all of the runs.  So if you're performing a more targeted experiment (e.g. a targeted SRM experiment) where you expect a majority of the proteins to change in concentration across conditions, median normalization is not ideal because it may remove the biological effects that you intended to study.  

I would take a look at the table in step 20 of section "Procedure 1: MSstatsShiny analysis pipeline" in this paper.  For each normalization method within MSstats, it documents the experiment assumptions to consider before employing the method. 

Tony

messages.author: 3f7dab23a7bc0436
messages.subject: Re: batch effect MSstats handled ?
parts:
Hi,

I would advise against applying normalization separately.  If you normalize data separately for each group, you eliminate both technical and biological differences within those groups. However, this leaves the differences between groups intact. This imbalance can make it look like the groups are more different than they actually are, artificially lowering your p-values and leading to an increased number of false positives in your results.

For cases where you expect protein abundance to change for a majority of proteins across conditions, we recommend applying reference-based normalization, i.e. for each run, add a known amount of spike-in reference peptide and normalize with respect to the spike-in reference peptide intensity value.  Of course, this would require you to design your experiment ahead of time to use a spike-in reference peptide. 

Tony
